title: Magnetic control of Goos-Hänchen shifts and group delay time in monolayer WSe$_2$
authors: Youssef Fattasse, Rachid El Aitouni, Miloud Mekkaoui, Pablo Díaz, David Laroze, Ahmed Jellal
abstract: We study the influence of an external magnetic field on the Goos-Hänchen (GH) shift and the group delay time (GDT) in monolayer WSe$_2$ in the presence of a magnetic barrier. The transport properties of Dirac-like carriers are obtained by solving the effective low-energy Hamiltonian and evaluating the corresponding transmission amplitudes. The GH shift and the GDT are subsequently extracted from the phase of the transmission coefficient. We systematically analyze their dependence on the magnetic field strength, incident energy, angle of incidence, and barrier width, with particular emphasis on the spin and valley degrees of freedom associated with the $K$ and $K'$ valleys. Our results show that the magnetic barrier strongly modulates both the GH shift and the GDT, leading to oscillatory behavior and pronounced spin-valley-dependent transport characteristics. Remarkably, the magnetic field enables selective control of the lateral shift and traversal time of carriers for each spin and valley channel, allowing for tunable spatial and temporal separation of electronic wave packets. This provides a mechanism for manipulating fermionic trajectories after transmission through the barrier in a highly controllable manner. Such tunability opens promising avenues for designing nanoscale devices based on spin and valley filtering, as well as for potential applications in information storage and processing within spintronic and valleytronic platforms.
summary: This theoretical study examines the magnetic control over electron wave packet dynamics (GH shift and GDT) in monolayer WSe2 through a magnetic barrier. By solving an effective Hamiltonian, the authors demonstrate that external magnetic fields induce strong oscillations and spin/valley selectivity in these transport properties. This offers a promising pathway for designing highly controllable nanoscale devices for spintronics and valleytronics.
main_problem: The study investigates how an external magnetic field influences the Goos-Hänchen (GH) shift and group delay time (GDT) in monolayer WSe2 when a magnetic barrier is present.
main_result: The magnetic barrier strongly modulates both the GH shift and GDT, enabling selective control over the lateral shift and traversal time for individual spin and valley channels. This suggests a mechanism for tunable spatial and temporal separation of electronic wave packets.
method: Transport properties are calculated by solving an effective low-energy continuum Hamiltonian and extracting the GH shift and GDT from the phase of the transmission coefficient.
model_or_system: The system is monolayer WSe2 modeled using an effective low-energy Hamiltonian that incorporates spin-orbit coupling, Zeeman effects, and a magnetic barrier potential. The analysis treats charge carriers as Dirac-like fermions propagating through regions defined by this magnetic structure.
key_observables: Goos–Hänchen (GH) shift, Group Delay Time (GDT), transmission amplitudes, reflection/transmission probabilities.
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength ($B$), incident energy ($E$), angle of incidence ($\phi$), and barrier width ($D$ or $d$).
main_assumptions: The model uses an effective continuum approach; the magnetic field is realized via ferromagnetic strips creating a defined barrier region.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of normalized group delay time on the magnetic field for various incident energies and angles, showing oscillatory behavior.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model using an effective Hamiltonian, derives transmission coefficients by solving boundary value problems across pristine and barrier regions, and finally analyzes the phase-dependent observables (GH shift and GDT) to demonstrate magnetic control.
why_interesting: The ability to selectively manipulate spin and valley degrees of freedom via external fields in a 2D material is highly relevant for developing next-generation spintronic and valleytronic devices, connecting fundamental quantum transport theory to solid-state engineering.
